domain: Political Economy / Housing Markets / Institutional Analysis
topic_summary: Analysis of the contested commitment that 'housing prices are set by a natural law of supply and demand.' The naturalist reading treats price formation as a mountain (inevitable equilibrium, no beneficiaries). The institutional reading treats clearing prices as constructed by zoning, lending standards, tax policy, and platform intermediaries, with identifiable beneficiaries (incumbent owners, lenders, intermediaries) and victims (renters, first-time buyers). The contest is whether 'the market price' names a natural fact or an enforced allocation presented as one.

key_entities: Platform intermediaries / real estate industry (beneficiaries under institutional reading)
Zoning authorities (mechanism operators under institutional reading)
key_tensions: Natural equilibrium vs constructed allocation (naturalist vs institutional readings)
Price-taker assumption vs price-making power (market participant characterization)
key_absences: Land as distinct from improvements (classical political economy distinction)
Positional good dynamics (housing as relative status marker)
Intergenerational wealth transfer mechanism (inheritance/gift down payment)

Generated omega_georgist_mountain_claim to bound this uncertainty. Four readings selected based on distinct interpretive commitments that would emit structurally different constraints.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The commitment that 'housing prices are determined by supply and demand' — a shared substrate all parties argue about, but read differently in ways that change what it constrains and who benefits.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Economic orthodoxy (naturalist), institutional economics (institutional), classical political economy (georgist), heterodox finance theory (financialization). Authority grounded in disciplinary tradition and empirical interpretation.

readings.commitment: Price formation is a natural equilibrium process reflecting objective scarcity and preference
readings.expected_structural_delta: Mountain constraint: no beneficiaries, no victims, no extractiveness. Price is discovered, not constructed. Policy interventions create deadweight loss.

readings.commitment: Price formation is constructed by zoning, lending standards, tax treatment, and intermediary platforms
readings.expected_structural_delta: Tangled rope: identifiable beneficiaries (incumbent owners, lenders, intermediaries) and victims (renters, first-time buyers). Extractiveness moderate to high depending on regulatory restrictiveness.

readings.commitment: Price formation separates land rent (unearned, location-based) from improvement value (earned, labor/capital-based)
readings.authority_grounding: Classical political economy / land value taxation tradition
readings.expected_structural_delta: Hybrid: land component is mountain (fixed supply, location scarcity), but rent capture is snare (landowners extract from labor without producing). Improvement component is rope (coordination of production).

readings.commitment: Price formation is driven by credit expansion, asset-price feedback loops, and housing-as-financial-asset demand
readings.authority_grounding: Heterodox finance theory / Minsky-Keen credit dynamics
readings.expected_structural_delta: Tangled rope with high extractiveness: financial sector benefits from credit expansion and transaction volume; households bear debt service and crash risk. Price level decoupled from shelter value, driven by leverage availability.

axiom_contradictions.basis: Naturalist axiom (prices are discovered facts) and institutional axiom (prices are constructed allocations) cannot both be true. If price is constructed, it is not discovered; if discovered, construction is epiphenomenal.

Naturalist treats all price components as earned returns to scarcity/productivity. Georgist axiom that land rent is unearned contradicts this — no framework holds both 'all returns are earned' and 'land returns are unearned' simultaneously.

Naturalist axiom (price reflects real scarcity/preference) contradicts financialization axiom (price reflects credit availability and speculative feedback). If price is credit-driven, it does not reflect real scarcity; if it reflects real scarcity, credit is neutral.
